passage:
Hansa had worked in the hospital's billing office for eight months when she started keeping a list in the back of her diary.
Monthly revenue target: up forty percent, with no new beds.
Santosh from pharmacy, who had asked why some patients were billed for tests they never had, now worked the Sunday shift alone and had been dropped from the team group.
At the weekly meeting, when a junior said a ward was short-staffed, the manager cut her off: 'Solutions, not problems.' Nobody raised anything after that.
And the joke by the water cooler, repeated with a wink: 'Curiosity killed the cat. Don't be a cat.'
Hansa read the list over on the bus home. Each item alone seemed small. Together, they looked like a pattern she didn't like at all.

qa.q: What happened to Santosh after he questioned the billing?
qa.a: Santosh now worked the Sunday shift alone and had been dropped from the team group.

qa.q: What does Hansa realise when she reads her list on the bus?
qa.a: She realises that things which seemed small alone form a worrying pattern together, and she feels uneasy about it.

qa.q: What could Hansa do with her list at this stage?
qa.a: She could keep the notes factual and dated, check in quietly with Santosh, and look for a safe channel, such as a compliance or patient-welfare office, to raise the pattern.

qa.q: How might the junior who was cut off feel at the next meeting?
qa.a: She is likely to feel silenced and wary, deciding it is safer not to bring bad news again.

grounding: It shows a colleague noticing warning signs of drift: impossible targets, an honest worker sidelined, bad news shut down and jokes about not asking questions.

passage:
Subject: am I reading too much into this?
Dear Gopika,
You always said to trust the small signals, so here are mine from the new job.
Our sales target doubled this quarter, but the product and the number of leads are the same. My manager says, 'Find a way.' Nobody asks how.
Farah, who flagged that parents were being promised refunds the policy doesn't allow, got moved to 'special projects', which means a desk by the printer and no calls.
When the refund numbers came in bad, the report to head office just didn't include them.
And there's a running joke: 'What happens in Q3 stays in Q3.'
Maybe every company is like this. But it feels like the air is slowly changing, and I'm the only one who smells it.
Sangeeta

qa.q: Where was Farah moved after flagging the refund promises?
qa.a: Farah was moved to 'special projects', a desk by the printer and no calls.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta mean by being 'the only one who smells it'?
qa.a: Sangeeta feels uneasy and alone, sensing a change in the workplace that nobody else seems willing to name.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta do next with these observations?
qa.a: Keep factual notes of the target, Farah's move and the missing refund figures, and find a safe person or channel to raise them with rather than waiting.

qa.q: What might Farah be experiencing at the desk by the printer?
qa.a: Farah is probably feeling sidelined and punished for honesty, cut off from the calls that used to be the job.

grounding: It shows a new employee spotting signs of drift: a target beyond honest means, an honest colleague sidelined, bad news left out and jokes about secrecy.

passage:
You want to know when I realised something was wrong at the company? It wasn't one thing. It was a pattern.
Our quarterly targets were double what the market could give, and somehow the sales team kept hitting them. In meetings nobody brought bad news; the one time someone did, the director went cold for a week. There was a running joke: "Don't ask, don't audit." Everyone laughed.
Then there was Nirmala. Best analyst on our floor. She flagged that some sales looked as if they'd been booked twice. The next month she was "restructured" into a back-office role. People stopped sitting with her at lunch, as if she were contagious.
That's when I started keeping notes: dates, who said what. I'm Chaitanya. I didn't know yet what I'd do. But I knew I'd seen enough to stop pretending I hadn't.

qa.q: What was the running joke?
qa.a: Don't ask, don't audit.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya feel when Nirmala was restructured?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt uneasy and alarmed, recognising a pattern in which honest people were punished.

qa.q: Why is Chaitanya's note-keeping a wise step?
qa.a: It records the signs of drift, impossible targets, fear of bad news and sidelining, so any later concern rests on facts.

qa.q: What is it like for Nirmala after being restructured?
qa.a: Nirmala feels isolated and punished, avoided at lunch for flagging a real problem.

grounding: A colleague notices impossible targets, fear of bad news, jokes about not asking and an honest analyst sidelined.

passage:
I'm Afreen. I sit two desks from Harish in the claims department, and I've watched what has happened to him this year.
In March he refused to approve a batch of claims that didn't match the hospital bills. He wrote a polite note explaining why. Our manager thanked him in the meeting, then gave the batch to someone else, who approved it the same afternoon.
Since then Harish hasn't been given a single complex case. His promotion "needs another cycle". At Friday tea someone joked, "Don't be a Harish," and everyone laughed, including our manager.
Meanwhile our targets keep rising, far beyond what honest processing could manage, and in meetings nobody says anything that sounds like bad news. I don't know exactly how Harish feels. He still comes in on time and says good morning to everyone. But he eats lunch alone now, and he has stopped writing notes.

qa.q: What did Harish refuse to approve in March?
qa.a: A batch of claims that didn't match the hospital bills.

qa.q: What does Afreen feel hearing the joke 'Don't be a Harish'?
qa.a: Afreen feels uneasy and troubled, seeing an honest colleague mocked while rules are quietly ignored.

qa.q: What could Afreen do with what has been observed?
qa.a: Keep a record of the pattern, quietly check in with Harish, and consider raising it through a proper channel.

qa.q: What might Harish be going through now?
qa.a: Harish likely feels isolated and discouraged, sidelined and eating alone after doing the right thing.

grounding: A colleague watches an honest claims officer sidelined, rules quietly ignored, targets set beyond honest means and jokes about questioning.

passage:
Week 1. At the Monday meeting, Tushar noticed that the regional head set a target forty per cent higher than last year, in a market that had shrunk. Nobody objected.
Week 4. Arohi, the most careful accountant on the floor, raised a question about a supplier's invoices. The head said, "Arohi, we need solutions, not problems." People laughed nervously.
Week 7. Arohi was moved off the supplier account. A colleague whispered at the coffee machine, "Rule one here: don't ask too many questions." Tushar realised he had heard that joke three times that month.
Week 9. At the review every team reported green. No one mentioned the missing documents Tushar had seen with his own eyes. Walking to the metro, he felt a cold weight in his stomach. The honest ones were being pushed aside, and the rest of them, including him, were learning to stay quiet.

qa.q: How much higher was the target than last year?
qa.a: Forty per cent higher.

qa.q: What did Tushar feel walking to the metro in week 9?
qa.a: He felt a cold, uneasy weight, realising he too was learning to stay quiet.

qa.q: What step could Tushar take now?
qa.a: Write down the pattern he has seen, check in with Arohi, and look for a proper channel to raise the concern.

qa.q: What might Arohi feel after being moved off the account?
qa.a: Arohi likely feels sidelined and discouraged, punished for asking a careful question.

grounding: Over weeks a colleague notices targets beyond legitimate means, fear of bad news, jokes about questions and an honest accountant sidelined.

passage: "Sit, Chetan. You asked why I always ask about a company's targets before anything else. When I was twenty-five, a young woman at a pharmaceutical distributor in Chennai, I started to notice things. The targets doubled one year, and nobody could explain how we would reach them honestly. The one colleague who kept asking, a quiet man named Sampath, was moved to the stores. At lunch, people joked, 'Don't be a Sampath, don't ask too much.' When a shipment came back from a hospital, the manager said, 'Bring me good news only.' I laughed at the jokes too, at first. Then one evening I sat alone in the canteen, counted those signs on a paper napkin, and felt cold. Three signs in one year. That napkin is why I left before the audit came. Your Rukmini Amma is telling you, Chetan: watch the jokes. They tell you what people are afraid to say."

qa.q: Where was Sampath moved?
qa.a: Sampath was moved to the stores.

qa.q: What did Rukmini feel when she counted the signs on the napkin?
qa.a: Rukmini felt cold with alarm, suddenly seeing that the jokes and targets she had laughed along with were warning signs.

qa.q: In the story, which choice changed things, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Sitting alone and writing the signs on a napkin let Rukmini see the pattern clearly, which is why she left before the audit came.

qa.q: How might Sampath have experienced those jokes at lunch?
qa.a: Sampath was probably hurt and isolated, hearing his honesty turned into a warning to others while he sat in the stores.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing the signs of organisational drift: honest people sidelined, impossible targets, fear of bad news and jokes about asking questions.
